decision: Apply the named Isegran island geometry as the canonical anchor because the place combines fortification, naval-harbour, shipyard, museum-harbour and vessel-preservation layers.
identityFindings: Isegran is a small named island where Glomma divides into Østerelva and Vesterelva.
The place record combines several components on the same island: fortifications, former naval harbour, shipyard history, museum harbour and current vessel preservation.
A whole-island anchor is therefore more representative than a fort tower, ferry terminal, workshop address or one harbour point.
Isegran fort and the public ferry arrival remain separately mapped subanchors.
chronologyFindings: The name Isegran is known from a chronicle entry for 1287 associated with Alv Erlingsson and the killing of Hallkjell Krøkedans.
Fredrikstad municipality states that no archaeological evidence has yet confirmed the medieval castle traditionally associated with Alv Erlingsson.
Documented fortification remains and excavated layers primarily relate to the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.
The visible cylindrical tower wall was reconstructed in 1984–1988 from historical images and archaeological interpretation, then restored and opened as a viewpoint in 2025.
Isegran also served as a naval harbour and was used by Tordenskiold during the Great Northern War.
Bjarne Aas operated an important boatyard on Isegran in the first half of the twentieth century.
The current vessel-preservation centre continues maritime craft through restoration, new construction, rigging, bronze casting, documentation, courses and guided tours.

rejectedAlternatives.reason: Geographically close, but lacks a named source-object and component role.
Strong fort anchor but excludes the shipyard, museum-harbour and vessel-preservation layers in the place identity.
Represents the current maritime organisation and workshop access, not the island's full historical environment.
Useful public arrival anchor but not the cultural-environment identity.

representationLimits: The marker represents the island cultural environment rather than one building or fortification component.
Year 1287 is a first-reference and event layer, not proof of a surviving medieval castle.
The current tower is partly reconstructed and restored, not an untouched seventeenth-century structure.
Workshops, vessels, moorings and event areas may have rules or restricted access distinct from public island paths.
The radius is not an island, fortification, harbour, workshop, property, event or safety boundary.
